Pet products need regular cleaning to maintain hygiene. Look for products with smooth surfaces, removable parts, or dishwasher-safe components. Products that are difficult to clean can become breeding grounds for bacteria.

Regular Cleaning Schedule

Inspect for Wear and Tear

Periodically examine your pet's products for signs of damage —frayed edges, loose parts, or cracking. Addressing minor issues early can prevent costly replacements and, more importantly, keep your pet safe from potential injuries.

Storage When Not in Use

If the product is seasonal or occasionally used, store it in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Proper storage prevents material degradation and keeps the product in good condition for years to come.

Bringing a kitten into your home is one of the most joyful experiences a cat owner can have —but with that joy comes serious responsibility. Kittens grow at an astonishing rate during their first year, roughly doubling their birth weight in just the first two weeks and reaching near-adult size by 10—2 months. To support this incredible development, they need a diet that is specifically formulated for their nutritional needs. Not just any cat food will do.

Don't pay extra for marketing, though — check the label for a statement that the food is formulated for growth or all life stages. That line matters more than the photos of salmon on the bag.

Feed on a schedule, not free-choice, if you can. Kittens under six months need three to four small meals a day because their stomachs are tiny and their growth demands are enormous. By twelve months, most cats can move to two meals and adult food. Choosing the right kitten food is one of the most important decisions you'll make for your new companion. The wrong diet can lead to developmental problems, a weakened immune system, and lifelong health complications. The right one? It sets the foundation for a vibrant, energetic, and long life.

Why Kitten Food Is Different from Adult Cat Food

Kittens are not simply small cats —they are in a completely different life stage. Their bodies demand higher levels of protein, fat, calories, and specific vitamins and minerals to support rapid muscle growth, bone development, and brain maturation. Adult cat food simply doesn't deliver enough of these critical nutrients.

Here is what sets kitten food apart:

  • Higher calorie density: Kittens burn energy faster than adults. Kitten food typically contains 350—50 kcal per 100g, compared to 250—50 kcal in adult formulas.
  • Elevated protein: Kittens need at least 30—0% protein on a dry matter basis for optimal muscle development.
  • DHA enrichment: Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is an omega-3 fatty acid critical for brain and vision development —a non-negotiable ingredient in any quality kitten food.
  • Calcium and phosphorus: Proper ratios of these minerals (typically 1.0:1 to 1.5:1) are essential for healthy bone and tooth formation.
  • Smaller kibble size: Designed for tiny mouths and developing teeth.

Most veterinarians recommend feeding kittens a complete kitten formula until they are at least 12 months old, though large breed kittens may need to continue until 18—4 months.

How to Transition Your Kitten to New Food

Never switch your kitten's food abruptly. A sudden change can cause digestive upset, diarrhea, and refusal to eat. Follow this 7-day transition plan:

  • Days 1-2: 75% old food + 25% new food
  • Days 3-4: 50% old food + 50% new food
  • Days 5-6: 25% old food + 75% new food
  • Day 7: 100% new food

Monitor your kitten's stool quality throughout the transition. Loose stools or vomiting are signs to slow down the transition. If problems persist beyond a few days, consult your veterinarian.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

cat food for kittens essential nutrition for growing cats

When should I switch from kitten food to adult cat food?

Most kittens should transition to adult cat food at 12 months of age. However, large-breed kittens (such as Maine Coons or British Shorthairs) may need to stay on kitten food until 18—4 months, as their growth period is extended. Always consult your veterinarian for personalized guidance based on your kitten's breed, size, and health status.

Can I feed my kitten adult cat food in an emergency?

In a genuine emergency, a single meal of adult cat food is unlikely to cause harm. However, adult cat food lacks the elevated protein, fat, and DHA levels that kittens require for proper development. Do not make it a habit. Visit a pet store or contact your vet for a proper kitten food option as soon as possible.

Should I feed my kitten wet food, dry food, or both?

Both wet and dry food have advantages. Wet food provides additional moisture, which is beneficial for urinary tract health, and many kittens find it more palatable. Dry food is convenient, helps mechanically clean teeth, and can be left out for free-feeding. Most veterinarians and nutritionists recommend a combination of both for the most balanced nutrition. Always ensure fresh water is available regardless of food type.

How much should I feed my kitten?

Follow the feeding guidelines on the food packaging as a starting point, but remember that every kitten is different. Kittens of the same age can have dramatically different caloric needs based on their activity level, metabolism, and size. Use the body condition score as your guide —you should be able to feel (but not see) your kitten's ribs. If you're unsure, your veterinarian can help you determine the right portion size.

Why is DHA important for kittens?

DHA (docosahexaenoic acid) is an omega-3 fatty acid that plays a critical role in the development of the brain, nervous system, and vision. Kittens whose mothers received DHA supplementation during pregnancy and nursing —and who continue to receive it in their own diet —show measurable improvements in cognitive function and visual acuity. This is why reputable kitten formulas always include DHA.

My kitten is a picky eater. What should I do?

Picky eating can be frustrating. Try warming the food slightly (to body temperature) to enhance aroma, mixing wet and dry food together, or adding a small amount of warm water to dry food to create a p芒t茅-like texture. If your kitten consistently refuses to eat for more than 24 hours, consult your veterinarian, as appetite loss can indicate underlying illness.

Are grain-free diets safe for kittens?

Yes, grain-free diets are generally safe for kittens as long as they are nutritionally complete and balanced. Grain-free does not automatically mean healthier —what matters most is the overall nutritional profile. However, if your kitten has a diagnosed grain allergy or sensitivity, a grain-free option like Blue Buffalo or Orijen can be an excellent choice. Always ensure the formula is AAFCO-certified for kitten growth.

Final Thoughts

The first year of your kitten's life is the most critical period for physical and neurological development. What you feed them during this time will shape their health trajectory for years —possibly decades —to come. Investing in a high-quality kitten food is one of the smartest, most loving decisions you can make as a new cat owner.

Our top recommendation, Royal Canin Kitten Food, offers the most comprehensive and scientifically validated formula for kittens of all breeds. For budget-conscious families, Hill's Science Diet Kitten delivers exceptional nutrition at a reasonable price. And for those seeking a natural, whole-ingredient approach, Blue Buffalo Healthy Growth is an outstanding choice.

Whatever you choose, remember that every kitten is unique. Monitor their growth, energy levels, coat quality, and stool consistency —and maintain regular check-ups with your veterinarian. With the right nutrition, your tiny kitten will grow into a strong, healthy, and thriving adult cat.

Choosing the right hamster bedding is one of the most important decisions you'll make as a hamster owner. Your little companion spends the majority of their time on the cage floor, burrowing, nesting, and exploring — and the material beneath their paws plays a massive role in their health, happiness, and overall quality of life. The wrong bedding can cause respiratory issues, skin irritation, eye problems, and even serious injuries. The right one? It turns a simple cage into a cozy, enriching home.

In this guide, we break down everything you need to know about hamster bedding in 2026, including what to avoid, what to look for, and our top five recommended products for every budget and cage setup.

Since this guide first went up, the biggest change in hamster bedding is availability of paper options in deeper-value packs, which matters because the current welfare standard calls for deep bedding — at least 8 to 10 inches of it — so your hamster can actually tunnel like it would in the wild. The wood warning still stands, and it's worth repeating: cedar and untreated pine contain phenols that damage a hamster's respiratory system over time. The RSPCA lists aspen as the safe wood option. If your hamster sneezes, squints, or sounds raspy after a bedding change, switch back to paper and call an exotic vet — respiratory infections in hamsters move fast.

Why Bedding Matters More Than You Think

Hamsters are burrowing animals by nature. In the wild, they dig elaborate tunnel systems to escape predators and regulate temperature. In captivity, they express this instinct by creating nests, burrowing, and rearranging their bedding constantly. Poor quality or unsafe bedding can:

  • Cause respiratory infections from dusty or aromatic materials
  • Lead to impacted cheek pouches if ingested
  • Create skin irritation and fur loss
  • Trap ammonia from urine, leading to urinary tract issues
  • Fail to absorb moisture, creating a damp, bacteria-friendly environment

According to the RSPCA and PDSA, dust-free, absorbent, and non-toxic bedding is essential for hamster welfare. Avoid any cedar or pine shavings (even "kiln-dried"), corn cob bedding, and scented products.

What to Look for in Hamster Bedding

  • Dust-free or low-dust: Dust particles are the #1 cause of respiratory problems in hamsters. Look for bedding specifically labeled dust-free.
  • High absorbency: The bedding should wick moisture away and neutralize odors effectively.
  • Safe ingredients: No added fragrances, dyes, or chemicals. All-natural is best.
  • Appropriate texture: Fine, soft fibers are best for burrowing. Large, hard pieces can injure small feet.
  • Odor control: Natural odor control without artificial scents is ideal.

Its fluffy, cloud-like consistency provides excellent cushioning for delicate hamster paws and makes burrowing a delight. The small fiber size also means it compacts well, reducing the amount of bedding needed per cage clean while still maintaining excellent absorbency.

Materials to Absolutely Avoid

Not all bedding is created equal, and some common options are genuinely dangerous for hamsters:

  • Cedar and Pine Shavings: Even "kiln-dried" shavings contain harmful aromatic phenols (aromatic hydrocarbons) that can cause liver disease and respiratory damage in small rodents. Avoid all cedar and most pine shavings.
  • Corn Cob Bedding: While sometimes marketed as natural, corn cob is prone to mold when wet, can impact hamster cheek pouches if eaten, and offers poor absorbency.
  • Cat Litter: Clumping cat litter is extremely dangerous — if ingested or even touched with wet paws, it can cause fatal intestinal blockages.
  • Scented Bedding: Artificial fragrances mask odor but don't address it, and the chemicals can damage delicate hamster respiratory systems.
  • Newspaper/Printed Paper: Ink contains toxic compounds (especially from traditional petroleum-based inks), and the slick surface is uncomfortable for hamster paws.
  • Fabric or Cotton Fluff: "Fluffy" pet bedding can wrap around hamster limbs, causing circulation loss and injury. Long fibers also pose an impaction risk if ingested.

How Much Bedding Should You Use?

Hamsters need deep bedding to exhibit natural burrowing behavior. The minimum recommended depth is 6 inches (15 cm), with 10+ inches (25+ cm) being ideal for Syrian hamsters. Dwarf hamsters can manage with slightly less, but deeper is always better. Not only does deep bedding support natural behaviors, but it also helps regulate cage humidity and reduces the frequency of full substrate changes.

For a standard 40-gallon breeder tank or a typical syrian hamster cage (100cm x 50cm), plan on using approximately 10-15 liters of bedding to achieve a 6-inch depth across the majority of the cage floor. Add more in areas where your hamster likes to nest.

FAQ — Frequently Asked Questions About Hamster Bedding

Q: How often should I completely change the hamster bedding?

A: With high-quality, absorbent paper bedding and proper spot-cleaning, you can typically go 3-4 weeks between full cage cleans. Remove soiled bedding daily or every other day, and stir/fluff the remaining bedding to redistribute moisture and extend its life. If you notice a persistent ammonia smell before the 3-week mark, do a full change regardless.

Q: Can I mix different types of bedding?

A: Yes, many hamster owners mix paper bedding with other safe substrates like aspen shavings (NOT pine or cedar), coco fiber, or hemp bedding to improve texture and cost efficiency. Just ensure the majority of the mix is safe, dust-free paper bedding, and avoid mixing in any unsafe materials.

Q: Is white or colored paper bedding better?

A: Natural white paper bedding is generally preferred because it contains no added dyes and makes it easier to spot-clean soiled areas. Colored bedding from reputable brands uses food-grade dyes that are considered safe, but white remains the cleaner choice. Avoid bright or dark colored bedding from unknown manufacturers.

Q: My hamster is eating the paper bedding. Is this dangerous?

A: Paper bedding is non-toxic and passing small amounts through the digestive tract is not usually dangerous. However, if your hamster is consuming large quantities of bedding, it could indicate boredom, inadequate nutrition, or stress. Make sure your hamster has a varied, nutritious diet, plenty of enrichment, and that the cage is appropriately sized (minimum 450 sq inches of floor space, though 800+ is ideal).

Q: What about "odor control" additives in bedding?

A: Products like Carefresh use activated carbon or natural plant extracts to neutralize odor without artificial fragrances. These are generally safe and effective. However, avoid any bedding that lists "fragrance" or "parfum" as an ingredient, as these synthetic additives can harm hamster respiratory health.

Q: Can I use fleece liners instead of loose bedding?

A: Fleece liners are popular for Syrian hamster cages, but they should never be the sole substrate. Hamsters are burrowing animals who need deep, loose substrate for nesting and tunneling. Fleece can be used as a base layer under paper bedding, or in specific areas, but at least 50% of the cage floor should always be covered with deep, loose, safe bedding.

Q: Is aspen bedding safe for hamsters?

A: Yes, aspen shavings are considered safe for hamsters. Unlike pine and cedar, aspen does not contain harmful aromatic phenols. However, aspen is less absorbent than paper bedding and can be rougher on delicate paws. Many hamster owners use aspen as a mixing substrate alongside paper bedding for added texture and cost savings. Always ensure aspen is dust-free and from a reputable source.

Introduction

Parrots are intelligent, long-lived companions that require specialized nutrition to thrive. Unlike cats or dogs, these colorful birds have unique dietary needs that reflect their diverse natural habitats-from tropical rainforests to arid savannas. Providing proper nutrition is one of the most important responsibilities of parrot ownership, directly impacting your bird's health, longevity, and quality of life.

In this guide to the best parrot food in 2026, we'll explore the different types of parrot diets, compare top-rated products, and provide expert recommendations to help you make informed choices for your feathered friend. Whether you have a tiny budgie or a majestic macaw, understanding parrot nutrition is essential for raising a healthy, happy bird.

Quick 2026 update: pellet formulas have gotten noticeably better this year. Several brands we follow switched to cold-pressed manufacturing, which preserves more of the heat-sensitive vitamins that regular extruded pellets lose during processing. If your bird has been on the same pellet for years, it's worth checking whether the formula changed or a better version now exists — birds on all-seed diets still develop the same fatty liver and vitamin A problems vets have warned about for decades. The Association of Avian Veterinarians continues to recommend pellets as 50-70% of a parrot's diet, with fresh vegetables and limited seeds making up the rest.

One practical tip we've picked up since first publishing this guide: transition pellets slowly. Mix the new pellet into the old one over two to three weeks rather than swapping overnight. Parrots are suspicious of new food colors, and a bird that refuses to eat can go downhill fast. Weigh your bird weekly during the switch with a gram scale — a loss of more than 10% means slow down.

Understanding Parrot Nutrition Basics

Parrots are classified as hookbills due to their curved, hooked beaks designed for cracking seeds and nuts. In the wild, parrots consume an incredibly varied diet that includes seeds, nuts, fruits, vegetables, flowers, insects, and even clay for mineral supplementation. This dietary diversity provides all the nutrients they need for energy, growth, and reproduction.

When kept as pets, parrots rely entirely on their owners to provide balanced nutrition. Unfortunately, many well-meaning bird owners inadvertently malnourish their pets by feeding all-seed diets or inappropriate foods. Understanding the fundamental components of parrot nutrition is the first step toward optimal health.

Key Nutritional Requirements

Proteins: Essential for muscle development, feather production, and immune function. Parrots typically need 10-15% protein in their diet, though breeding birds and growing chicks require higher amounts.

Fats: Provide concentrated energy and essential fatty acids for healthy skin and feathers. However, excess fat leads to obesity, a common problem in pet parrots. Aim for 5-10% fat content in the overall diet.

Carbohydrates: The primary energy source for parrots. Complex carbohydrates from whole grains and vegetables are preferred over simple sugars.

Vitamins: Vitamin A is essential for respiratory health and vision, while vitamins D3, E, and B-complex vitamins support various metabolic functions. Many pelleted diets include supplemental vitamins.

Minerals: Calcium is particularly important for egg-laying females and growing birds. Other essential minerals include phosphorus, magnesium, and trace elements like zinc and selenium.

Water: Often overlooked but absolutely critical. Fresh, clean water must be available at all times. Parrots can become dehydrated quickly, especially in warm environments.

Types of Parrot Food

Pellets: The Foundation of Modern Parrot Nutrition

Pelleted diets have revolutionized parrot nutrition since their introduction in the 1980s. These scientifically formulated foods contain a precise blend of grains, proteins, vitamins, and minerals, ensuring that every bite provides complete nutrition. Unlike seeds, pellets prevent selective feeding-a common problem where birds pick out favorite seeds and ignore less palatable but nutritionally important ones.

Advantages of Pellets:

  • Complete and balanced nutrition in every bite
  • Prevent selective feeding behavior
  • Lower fat content than seed-based diets
  • Fortified with essential vitamins and minerals
  • Longer shelf life than fresh foods
  • Less mess and waste

Considerations:

  • Some birds initially resist pellets and require conversion training
  • Lower in natural variety and enrichment value
  • Quality varies significantly between brands
  • Cannot be the sole diet-fresh foods should still be offered

Seeds: The Traditional but Flawed Choice

For decades, seed mixes were the default diet for pet parrots. While seeds can be part of a balanced diet, they should never be the exclusive food source. Sunflower seeds and safflower seeds-common components of commercial mixes-are high in fat and low in essential nutrients. An all-seed diet leads to malnutrition, obesity, and shortened lifespans.

Appropriate Uses for Seeds:

  • Training rewards and positive reinforcement
  • Foraging enrichment activities
  • Small portion of overall diet (no more than 10-20%)
  • Transitioning birds from all-seed diets to pellets

Quality Seed Mixes Should Include:

  • Varied seed types (millet, canary seed, oats)
  • Dried fruits and vegetables
  • Nuts in moderation
  • No artificial colors or preservatives

Fresh Foods: Essential Variety and Enrichment

No parrot diet is complete without fresh fruits and vegetables. These foods provide natural vitamins, minerals, antioxidants, and fiber while offering important behavioral enrichment. Chewing and manipulating fresh foods satisfies natural foraging instincts and prevents boredom.

Safe Vegetables for Parrots:

  • Dark leafy greens (kale, spinach, collard greens)
  • Bell peppers (all colors)
  • Carrots and sweet potatoes
  • Broccoli and cauliflower
  • Squash and zucchini

Species-Specific Considerations

Small Parrots (Budgies, Lovebirds, Parrotlets)

Small parrots have fast metabolisms and high energy needs. Choose appropriately sized pellets (crumbles or mini pellets) and offer finely chopped fresh vegetables. These species can become overweight on high-fat seed diets, so pellets are especially important.

Medium Parrots (Conures, Quakers, Senegals)

Medium parrots do well on standard-sized pellets and enjoy a variety of fresh foods. These intelligent birds benefit from foraging opportunities and may need diet variety to prevent boredom.

Large Parrots (African Greys, Amazons, Eclectus)

Large parrots require substantial amounts of food. African Greys are prone to calcium deficiency, so ensure adequate calcium through pellets and fresh greens. Eclectus parrots have unique digestive systems and do best on higher fiber diets with plenty of fresh produce.

Macaws and Cockatoos

These largest parrots need large pellets or multiple small pellets. Macaws require slightly higher fat content than other species-offer nuts in moderation. Cockatoos are prone to obesity, so monitor portions carefully and encourage exercise.

Converting Your Parrot to a Better Diet

Many parrots, especially those raised on all-seed diets, initially resist pellets. Patience and persistence are key to successful dietary conversion. Never simply remove all seeds and expect your bird to eat pellets immediately-this can lead to starvation.

Step-by-Step Conversion Guide

Week 1-2: Offer pellets alongside the usual seed diet. Your bird may ignore them initially, but this introduces the new food.

Week 3-4: Begin mixing pellets into the seed mix, gradually increasing the pellet proportion. Start with 25% pellets, 75% seeds.

Week 5-6: Increase to 50% pellets, monitoring your bird's intake and weight closely.

Week 7-8: Aim for 75% pellets, 25% seeds.

Week 9+: Transition to primarily pellets (70-80% of diet) with seeds as treats only.

Conversion Tips:

  • Weigh your bird weekly to ensure they're eating enough
  • Offer pellets in different locations-some birds prefer foraging from the cage floor
  • Try moistening pellets slightly to enhance aroma
  • Eat pellets in front of your bird; parrots are social learners
  • Be patient-conversion can take 2-3 months for stubborn birds

Feeding Schedule and Portions

Establishing a consistent feeding routine helps your parrot feel secure and makes it easier to monitor food intake. Most parrots benefit from two main meals per day, with fresh foods offered in the morning and pellets available throughout the day.

Recommended Daily Portions

Small Parrots (30-100g body weight): 1-2 teaspoons pellets, small amounts of fresh vegetables daily

Medium Parrots (100-400g body weight): 1-2 tablespoons pellets, fresh vegetables daily, small amounts of fruit

Large Parrots (400-800g body weight): 2-4 tablespoons pellets, generous fresh vegetables daily, moderate fruit

Macaws and Cockatoos (800g+ body weight): 1/4 to 1/2 cup pellets, large portions of fresh vegetables daily

Remember that these are guidelines-adjust portions based on your bird's activity level, age, and body condition. Consult your avian veterinarian for personalized recommendations.

Common Nutritional Problems in Pet Parrots

Obesity

Obesity is one of the most common health issues in pet parrots, typically caused by high-fat seed diets and insufficient exercise. Obese birds are at risk for fatty liver disease, heart problems, and shortened lifespans. Prevention includes feeding a balanced pellet-based diet, limiting high-fat treats, and providing opportunities for flight and exercise.

Vitamin A Deficiency

Common in birds fed all-seed diets, vitamin A deficiency leads to respiratory infections, poor feather quality, and weakened immune function. Symptoms include nasal discharge, sneezing, and white plaques in the mouth. Feeding dark leafy greens and orange vegetables, along with quality pellets, prevents this condition.

Calcium Deficiency

Especially problematic for African Greys and egg-laying females, calcium deficiency can cause seizures, egg binding, and brittle bones. Provide calcium-rich foods like dark greens and ensure adequate vitamin D3 for calcium absorption. Cuttlebones offer supplemental calcium and beak conditioning.

Hypocalcemia in African Greys

African Grey parrots are uniquely prone to idiopathic calcium deficiency, even when dietary calcium appears adequate. These birds may need calcium supplementation under veterinary guidance and should have calcium levels monitored regularly.

Storage and Food Safety

Proper food storage maintains nutritional quality and prevents spoilage or contamination:

  • Store pellets and seeds in airtight containers in cool, dry locations
  • Refrigerate opened bags of organic pellets
  • Discard any food that smells musty or shows signs of mold
  • Remove fresh foods from the cage after 2-4 hours to prevent spoilage
  • Wash all fresh produce thoroughly before serving
  • Never feed food from your mouth-human saliva contains bacteria harmful to birds
  • Clean food and water dishes daily with hot, soapy water

Signs of Good Nutrition

How do you know if your parrot's diet is meeting their needs? Look for these indicators of excellent nutritional health:

  • Bright, clear eyes without discharge or swelling
  • Smooth, glossy feathers with vibrant coloration
  • Clean, well-formed droppings (consisting of feces, urates, and urine)
  • Healthy body weight-you should be able to feel the keel bone but not see it prominently
  • High energy levels and natural curiosity
  • Strong beak and feet with healthy skin
  • Normal respiratory rate without tail bobbing or open-mouth breathing

Conversely, seek veterinary care if you notice poor feather quality, weight loss, lethargy, changes in droppings, or decreased appetite.

Conclusion

Providing optimal nutrition is one of the most impactful ways to ensure your parrot lives a long, healthy, and happy life. The best parrot food in 2026 combines scientifically formulated pellets as the dietary foundation with varied fresh fruits and vegetables for natural nutrients and behavioral enrichment. Seeds, while inappropriate as a primary diet, can be offered as training rewards and foraging opportunities in moderation.

Invest in high-quality pellets from reputable brands like Harrison's, Lafeber's, or Roudybush. Take time to transition your bird gradually if they're accustomed to seeds. Consult with an avian veterinarian to develop a feeding plan tailored to your parrot's species, age, and health status. With proper nutrition, your feathered companion can thrive for decades, bringing joy and companionship to your life.

Remember: you are what you eat-and so is your parrot. Choose wisely, feed thoughtfully, and enjoy the rewards of a healthy, vibrant bird.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can parrots eat only pellets?

While pellets provide complete nutrition, we recommend offering fresh vegetables and limited fruits alongside pellets. This provides behavioral enrichment, natural vitamins, and foraging opportunities that contribute to your bird's overall wellbeing.

How long do pellets stay fresh?

Properly stored in airtight containers, most pellets remain fresh for 2-3 months after opening. Organic varieties may have shorter shelf lives. Check for off odors or discoloration before feeding.

Should I give my parrot vitamin supplements?

If your parrot eats a quality pelleted diet with fresh foods, additional vitamin supplements are usually unnecessary and can even be harmful. Consult your avian veterinarian before adding supplements.

Can parrots eat human food?

Some human foods are safe for parrots in moderation, such as plain cooked chicken, whole grain bread, and unsweetened whole grain cereals. Always research before sharing human food, as many common foods are toxic to birds.

Why does my parrot throw food?

Food tossing can indicate several things: the food is unappealing, your bird is foraging naturally, or they're playing. Parrots are intelligent and can become bored-try offering variety and foraging opportunities.
